objects.description: 左上大型绘画复制图，中央蓝袍圣母怀抱婴儿，周围有多名天使，背景为金色装饰与羽翼。保留完整绘画画面，矩形显示，上缘贴画布边缘，不沿人物轮廓去背景。
右上竖向波斯细密画复制图，一名穿深蓝衣服的人弯腰，周围为金黄地面、植物和细小装饰，底部有画作自身的横向边饰。保留完整画面与原有绘画环境。
左下《戴珍珠耳环的少女》绘画复制图，单人头肩近景，少女戴蓝黄头巾，侧身回望，佩戴珍珠耳饰，背景近黑。显示窗口贴左侧及下侧画布边缘，保留绘画背景，不另拆人物。
材料栏内一块竖立的不规则蓝色青金石，顶部有浅色矿物部分，底部可见轻微投影。沿矿石整体外形独立显示，周围为白色，与下方标签分开。
材料栏下方左侧一堆深蓝色颜料粉末，主体呈低矮椭圆堆，左侧和上缘散落细小粉粒。完整粉堆及散粒属于同一摄影单元，沿外形显示在白色底上。
材料栏下方右侧一团深蓝色膏状油画颜料，表面有隆起、折叠与反光，底部可见淡淡投影。沿整团颜料的外形显示，周围为白色。
左上页码装饰，包含贴左边的红色实心矩形、浅灰色窄体数字“046”及向右延伸的淡红色折线。作为完整页眉设计保留。
右上页眉设计，包含细小灰色“ULTRAMARINE”、窄体页码“047”、淡红色折线和贴右边的红色矩形，整体保留。
材料介绍区域左侧与顶部的浅灰色细线，组成开放式直角栏界，不是照片窗口或照片边缘描边，作为独立版面装饰保留。
贯穿画面中部的蓝色横向笔刷设计：左端为截出画布的蓝色刷柄、银色金属箍和浅黄色刷毛，右接宽大的深蓝颜料笔触，边缘有细碎刷痕及不规则露白。刷子与连续笔触作为完整固定装饰保留。
右上纵向排列的四条深蓝色粗笔触色样，右端均延伸至画布边缘，颜色从近黑蓝到深群青，保留各条不规则笔刷边缘及条间白色空隙，作为一组色样设计。
右下纵向排列的四条蓝色粗笔触色样，右端贴画布边缘，由深蓝逐渐过渡为浅蓝，边缘带刷痕和不规则毛边，整体作为一组固定色样设计保留。

objects.text:
◁ Fit for a king
The holy icon of ultramarine
meant that only the very
wealthy could afford it.
Painters would specify where it
should be used on a painting.
This panel of the Virgin Mary
in her typical ultramarine
robes, and the infant Christ
was painted for Richard II of
England. The Wilton Diptych
(detail), Artist unknown,
c.1395–1399

Lapis lazuli contains a variety of minerals,
and the process required to extract blue
lazurite from the others is long and
complex. First, the lapis lazuli is ground
and mixed with resin, wax, soap, and
linseed oil to form a dough, which has
to be kneaded for up to 3 days. The
dough is then submerged in lye (a strong
alkali solution) until blue crystals separate
from it into liquid. These are separated,
dried, and ground to create a powder.
This is the pigment ultramarine.

△ True blue
Persian artists also used ultramarine for their
most important, eye-catching parts of a painting,
such as this drapery here. Detail of manuscript
from Herat in present-day Afghanistan, 1485

One of the most prized pigments in the history of
painting, deep blue ultramarine comes from the
semiprecious gemstone lapis lazuli, which means
“the blue stone” in Latin. For a long time, all the lapis
lazuli in Europe came from a single mountain range
in Afghanistan, the Sar-i Sang, which had been mined
for thousands of years. Despite the remote and
inaccessible location of this source, traders began
to import the precious material into Egypt as early as

◁ Catching the light
Ultramarine is made up of microscopic, finely ground, irregular
crystals that reflect light in many directions, giving the pigment
its luminosity, as seen in the headband here. Girl with a Pearl
Earring (detail), Johannes Vermeer, c.1665–1666

3000 BCE, mainly for use in jewelry. The arduous and
complicated method for turning lapis into usable paint
had not yet been discovered—the gemstone was hard
and difficult to grind, and unless its impurities were
removed, the resulting paint was dull and grayish.
The earliest successful examples of paint derived
from lapis lazuli have been found on 6th-century
Buddhist frescoes in Afghanistan. Its use spread
throughout the Middle East and Asia, but the
technique for extracting ultramarine did not really arrive
in Europe until the 1200s—in Italian it literally means
“beyond the sea.” Transportation costs, the difficulty
of extraction, and the small amounts of resulting
pigment made ultramarine the rarest and most
expensive pigment in medieval and Renaissance
art. At times, it was even more valuable than gold.
This precious pigment was therefore reserved for
the most important parts of a painting, such as the
heavens, and became particularly associated with

the Virgin Mary (notably her robes) from around
1400. During the High Renaissance, artists such
as Titian branched out beyond religious subjects,
creating compositions that made the most of
ultramarine’s luxurious vibrancy.
By the 1800s, scientists were trying to find an
alternative and affordable blue, and in 1828, a French
chemist developed a synthetic ultramarine that cost
only about one-tenth of the price of the natural
pigment. Although artists complained that “French
ultramarine” lacked the glorious luminosity of the
true pigment, by 1870, it was far more widely used.

▷ From dark to light
Ultramarine is a transparent and semi-
transparent pigment. Its strength is
when the pigment is concentrated or
lightened; it produces a deep, inky blue
field, but when it is lightened (bottom),
it becomes more sky blue in hue.
